stick_exercise_science_mets_calories_and.question: Exercise science - METs, calories and heart-rate zones, sealed
references: B. E. Ainsworth et al., 2011 Compendium of Physical Activities, Med. Sci. Sports Exerc. 43 (2011) 1575
H. Tanaka, K. D. Monahan, D. R. Seals, Age-predicted maximal heart rate revisited, J. Am. Coll. Cardiol. 37 (2001) 153
M. J. Karvonen, E. Kentala, O. Mustala, Ann. Med. Exp. Biol. Fenn. 35 (1957) 307
stick_exercise_science_mets_calories_and.statement: Energy cost and training intensity are arithmetic over three measured inputs: the activity's MET, the body's mass, and the heart's range.

ticks.claim: [running at 6 mph, SEALED] 9.8 MET (sealed through exercise_science.EX_VERIFY; Compendium code 12050). One MET is resting metabolism, 3.5 mL of oxygen per kg per minute; a ten-minute mile is nearly ten times rest.
[walking at 3 mph, SEALED] 3.3 MET (sealed through exercise_science.EX_VERIFY): a brisk walk is moderate intensity, the 3-6 MET band the guidelines name.
[sitting quietly, SEALED] 1.3 MET (sealed through exercise_science.EX_VERIFY): awake and still is a third above sleep's 0.95.
[a half-hour run, SEALED] 9.8 MET x 70 kg x 0.5 h = 343 kcal (sealed through exercise_science.EX_VERIFY): one MET-hour per kilogram is about one kilocalorie, so the product is the energy.
[an hour's walk, SEALED] 3.3 x 70 x 1 = 231 kcal (sealed through exercise_science.EX_VERIFY). The same hour, the same body, a third of the energy - intensity is what the MET measures.
[maximum heart rate at 30, SEALED] 208 - 0.7 x 30 = 187 bpm (sealed through exercise_science.EX_VERIFY; Tanaka 2001).
[at 40, SEALED] 208 - 28 = 180 bpm (sealed through exercise_science.EX_VERIFY) - where the old '220 - age' also says 180; the two lines cross at 40 and part on either side.
[at 60, SEALED] 208 - 42 = 166 bpm (sealed through exercise_science.EX_VERIFY); '220 - age' would say 160. Tanaka's shallower slope was fit to older adults the old rule underestimated.

[a Karvonen zone at 30, SEALED] Resting 60, maximum 187, reserve 127: the 50-70 percent zone is 60 + 0.5 x 127 = 124 to 60 + 0.7 x 127 = 149 bpm (sealed through exercise_science.EX_VERIFY). Karvonen (1957) scales the RESERVE, not the maximum, so a fit heart with a low resting rate trains in a wider band.
[at 50, SEALED] Resting 70, maximum 173, reserve 103: 60-80 percent is 132 to 152 bpm (sealed through exercise_science.EX_VERIFY).

[the inputs, CITED] A MET value is a population mean from the Compendium (Ainsworth 2011); the maximal heart rate 208 - 0.7 age is a regression across 351 studies with a standard deviation near 10 bpm (Tanaka 2001); 1 MET = 3.5 mL O2/kg/min = 1 kcal/kg/h is a convention. They work, so the numbers above are inferred from them, never kept as fact about one person - a measured VO2max or a stress test replaces the estimate. The engine seals the arithmetic and declines the prescription.
ticks.source: Ainsworth et al., MSSE 43 (2011) 1575; Tanaka et al., JACC 37 (2001) 153; Karvonen et al. (1957)

ticks.claim: [on the one map] The body at work is nutrition's ledger spent (card_floor_nutrition: the kilocalorie), physiology measured (card_floor_medicine: the heart's rate and reserve), and biology's metabolism (card_floor_biology: oxygen to work). Ties the nutrition and medicine sticks.
